content: A vegan diet excludes all animal products, focusing entirely on plant-based foods such as fruits, vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds. This dietary pattern can support health and reduce the risk of some chronic diseases. Major nutritional considerations include ensuring adequate intake of protein, vitamin B12, iron, calcium, omega-3 fatty acids, and certain other micronutrients less abundant or bioavailable in plant sources. Vitamin B12 is a critical concern because it is naturally found only in animal-derived foods, making supplementation or fortified foods essential for vegans. Plant-based protein can be sufficient when varied sources such as legumes, grains, nuts, and seeds are consumed. Iron from plant foods is non-heme and less efficiently absorbed, but absorption can be enhanced by vitamin C-rich foods and minimizing inhibitors like phytates during meals. Calcium needs can be met with fortified plant milks, leafy greens, and tofu made with calcium. Omega-3 fatty acids, especially EPA and DHA, can be obtained in limited amounts from algae-based supplements or by conversion from plant-based ALA sources. Practical application involves meal planning to ensure nutrient adequacy, awareness of potential nutrient gaps, and appropriate supplementation when needed. Limitations include variability in absorption and individual requirements. Understanding related concepts such as nutrient bioavailability, fortified foods, and supplements enhances success with this diet approach.
